explanation: Its curl circles the line for the G above middle C. The bass clef is the F clef: its two dots sit either side of the F line. Both shapes grew from letters.

claims.text: The treble clef is also called the G clef.
The F clef is the bass clef and the C clef is the alto and tenor clef; neither is the treble clef.
The curl of the treble clef circles the staff line of the G above middle C.
The two dots of the bass clef sit either side of the F line.
Clef shapes developed from stylized letters.

writerNotes: Self-check (§9.3). Lint: clean under content:check for writer w-pmusic01w. Claims: every checkable statement in the stem, options and explanation is listed, with risk at or above the C26 floor and raised where a fact is beyond everyday knowledge. Datasets: no pinned dataset covers these music facts (the manifest holds geographic, scientific, Nobel, Olympic and art-collection data), so each high-risk claim needs web evidence from the checkers. I used no WebSearch. Rival test: argued for the C clef, since middle C is the note most players know, and for the F clef; the treble clef's curl circles G, so the key stands. Three options on purpose: there are only three clef letters (G, F and C), so a fourth would be filler. Volatility: evergreen; no time words, and nothing depends on knowledge newer than mid-2026. Regional: the clefs are the same worldwide. Style: Oxford spelling, straight quotes, no en or em dashes, explanation within 35 words. Myths: screened against myths.json, no hit. Mystery: not applicable to a practice item. Encore: not applicable to a practice item. Doubts: None.
